entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9958"/><div sID="gen17708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9958"/><hi type="bold">16. send for--</hi>translate, "I will send many"; "I will give the commission to many" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7">2Ch 17:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fishers ... hunters--</hi>successive invaders of Judea (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Am 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Ha 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>). So "net" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>). As to "hunters," see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.9">Ge 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mi 7:2</reference>. The Chaldees were famous in hunting, as the Egyptians, the other enemy of Judea, were in fishing. "Fishers" expresses the ease of their victory over the Jews as that of the angler over fishes; "hunters," the keenness of their pursuit of them into every cave and nook. It is remarkable, the same image is used in a good sense of the Jews' restoration, implying that just as their enemies were employed by God to take them in hand for destruction, so the same shall be employed for their restoration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">Eze 47:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">10</reference>). So spiritually, those once enemies by nature (fishermen many of them literally) were employed by God to be heralds of salvation, "catching men" for life (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.19">Mt 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.10">Lu 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.41">Ac 2:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4:4</reference>); compare here <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jr 16:19</reference>, "the Gentiles shall come unto thee" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">2Co 12:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17709" type="x-p"/>

So "net" ( Eze 12:13 ). As to "hunters," see Ge 10:9 ; Mi 7:2 . The Chaldees were famous in hunting, as the Egyptians, the other enemy of Judea, were in fishing. "Fishers" expresses the ease of their victory over the Jews as that of the angler over fishes; "hunters," the keenness of their pursuit of them into every cave and nook. It is remarkable, the same image is used in a good sense of the Jews' restoration, implying that just as their enemies were employed by God to take them in hand for destruction, so the same shall be employed for their restoration ( Eze 47:9 , 10 ). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9960"/><div sID="gen17712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9960"/><hi type="bold">18. first ... double--</hi>Horsley translates, "I will recompense ... once and again"; literally, "the first time repeated": alluding to the two captivities--the Babylonian and the Roman. Maurer, "I will recompense their former iniquities (those long ago committed by their fathers) and their (own) repeated sins" (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.11">Jr 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.12">12</reference>). English Version gives a good sense, "First (before 'I bring them again into their land'), I will doubly (that is, fully and amply, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">Jr 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>) recompense."<div eID="gen17712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carcasses--</hi>not sweet-smelling sacrifices acceptable to God, but "carcasses" offered to idols, an offensive odor to God: human victims (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jr 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20">Eze 16:20</reference>), and unclean animals (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Is 65:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.17">66:17</reference>). Maurer explains it, "the carcasses" of the idols: their images void of sense and life. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jr 16:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.20">20</reference>. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Le 26:30</reference> favors this. <div eID="gen17713" type="x-p"/>

English Version gives a good sense, "First (before 'I bring them again into their land'), I will doubly (that is, fully and amply, Jr 17:18 ; Is 40:2 ) recompense." carcasses-- not sweet-smelling sacrifices acceptable to God, but "carcasses" offered to idols, an offensive odor to God: human victims ( Jr 19:5 ; Eze 16:20 ), and unclean animals ( Is 65:4 ; 66:17 ). Maurer explains it, "the carcasses" of the idols: their images void of sense and life. Compare Jr 16:19 , 20 . Le 26:30 favors this.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9961"/><div sID="gen17714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9961"/>19-20. The result of God's judgments on the Jews will be that both the Jews when restored, and the Gentiles who have witnessed those judgments, shall renounce idolatry for the worship of Jehovah. Fulfilled partly at the return from Babylon, after which the Jews entirely renounced idols, and many proselytes were gathered in from the Gentiles, but not to be realized in its fulness till the final restoration of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.17">Is 2:1-17</reference>). <div eID="gen17714" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 21. Therefore-- In order that all may be turned from idols to Jehovah, He will now give awful proof of His divine power in the judgments He will inflict. this once-- If the punishments I have heretofore inflicted have not been severe enough to teach them. my name ... Lord-- Jehovah ( Psa 83:18 ): God's incommunicable name, to apply which to idols would be blasphemy. Keeping His threats and promises ( Ex 6:3 ).
